query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, low-volume-fraction ductile Cu binder phase via post-solidification liquid metal infiltration will improve the structural integrity of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 by arresting microcrack propagation while preserving its large caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibiting excellent caloric performance but poor mechanical integrity with a propensity for cracking.
generation.intervention: Infiltrate a carefully controlled amount (approximately 5–10 vol%) of high-purity Cu into the as-solidified alloy by heating in an inert atmosphere to just above the melting point of Cu (around 1100°C) yet well below temperatures that might destabilize the MM′X phase, followed by controlled cooling to form an integrated ductile binder network.
generation.conditions: Processing under an inert (Ar) atmosphere to avoid oxidation; heat treatment temperature maintained near 1100°C for sufficient time to allow Cu infiltration without promoting excessive interdiffusion; operational conditions for caloric response remain at or near room temperature under applied-field and pressure-field cycling, and under standard compressive loading regimes.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an interconnected Cu phase along grain boundaries and as discrete binder regions that bridges microcracks and mitigates stress concentrations within the MM′X matrix.
generation.mechanism: The Cu binder network provides toughening by arresting crack propagation and redistributing applied stress, while its high thermal conductivity helps maintain efficient heat transport essential for the caloric effect. Because only a minor volume fraction is added, the intrinsic caloric phase remains largely unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant increase in mechanical integrity, with compressive strength anticipated to exceed the highest previously reported epoxy-containing sample (i.e., >218 MPa), alongside retention of the large caloric response (similar adiabatic temperature change and entropy change relative to the pristine alloy).
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy which shows excellent caloric performance but suffers from poor integrity and crack sensitivity.
generation.boundary: The Cu content must be limited to 5–10 vol% to avoid dilution of the caloric phase; processing temperatures/time must be strictly controlled to prevent harmful interdiffusion; the intervention must sustain performance under cyclic applied-field and pressure-field operation across the typical operating temperature range (room temperature to moderate elevations) and under representative mechanical loadings.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative effect on the caloric response remains uncertain and will likely require optimization of the Cu volume fraction and heat treatment parameters to balance integrity gains with retention of caloric performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples under identical conditions: one set with the proposed Cu infiltration and one baseline set without infiltration. Conduct compressive strength tests (and fracture toughness measurements) and measure the caloric properties (e.g., adiabatic temperature change and isothermal entropy change under applied-field and pressure-field cycling) for both sets. Complement the tests with microstructural characterization (SEM/EBSD) to confirm the formation and distribution of the Cu network.
measurements: Adiabatic temperature change under applied magnetic and pressure fields
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-infiltrated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (compressive strength >218 MPa) without a measurable degradation in the caloric response relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis will be rejected.
